title: When the Method Fools You: Pseudohyponatremia and Jaffe Creatinine
summary: Explain why indirect ISE reports falsely low sodium in severe lipemia or hyperproteinemia while direct ISE does not, and recognize positive and negative interferences in the Jaffe creatinine method.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 28 Hits 1–2 and Traps 1–2 (first lesson for Ch. 28). Checked against van Dongen 2026, Chopra 2026, Pottel 2024, Soleimani 2023 and Jiang 2026. Not taught: ultracentrifugation as a correction (Hit 1), Jaffe wavelength 490–500 nm, ferricyanide/surfactant mitigation, and aminoglycoside interference (Hit 2) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Contrast direct and indirect ISE and explain pseudohyponatremia.
List positive and negative interferences in the Jaffe creatinine method.
Choose the confirmatory method for each artefact.

scenes.title: A low sodium and a high creatinine that aren’t real
scenes.altText: Two invented reports. Patient 1: triglycerides 2,800 mg/dL, sodium 126 mmol/L on the main chemistry analyzer (indirect ISE), but 139 mmol/L on the blood-gas analyzer (direct ISE). Patient 2: diabetic ketoacidosis, creatinine 2.6 mg/dL by the Jaffe method, 1.1 mg/dL by an enzymatic method. Question token: “Which result is real — and why do the methods disagree?”

cues.text: A patient with triglycerides near 2,800 has a sodium of 126 on the main analyzer, but 139 on the blood-gas analyzer.
A second patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a creatinine of 2.6 by the Jaffe method, but 1.1 by an enzymatic method.
Which results are real, and why do the methods disagree?

props.label: Which is real? Why the gap?

scenes.title: Two ways to use an ion-selective electrode
scenes.altText: ISE card (Chopra 2026; van Dongen 2026): both use the same electrochemical principle. Direct ISE (blood-gas and many point-of-care analyzers) measures undiluted sample — the ion activity in plasma water. Indirect ISE (high-throughput chemistry analyzers) dilutes the sample first (dilution ratios ~1:5 to 1:46) and back-calculates the concentration assuming plasma is ~93% water. Schematic: a beaker of plasma — 93% water (sodium lives here), 7% lipids and proteins.

cues.text: Sodium is measured with an ion-selective electrode. Direct ISE, used in blood-gas and many point-of-care analyzers, measures the undiluted sample.
Indirect ISE, used on high-throughput chemistry analyzers, dilutes the sample first, by roughly 1 to 5 up to 1 to 46, then calculates back to the original concentration.
That back-calculation assumes plasma is about 93 percent water. Sodium dissolves only in the water.
Normally the assumption holds, and direct and indirect results agree.

scenes.title: When the water fraction shrinks
scenes.altText: Schematic beaker: with severe hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia, lipids/proteins occupy more volume, so plasma water falls below 93%. The sodium concentration in plasma water is unchanged (direct ISE stays normal), but indirect ISE — which assumes 93% water — reports a falsely low sodium: pseudohyponatremia (electrolyte exclusion effect). Data token (van Dongen 2026): in Intralipid-spiked samples, sodium bias exceeded analytical limits at a lipemic index of ~300 and CLIA allowable error at ~500, well below the manufacturer’s stated threshold (> 2,000); in clinical samples bias exceeded analytical limits above an L-index of ~100.

cues.text: Now add a lot of lipid or protein. They take up more of the plasma volume, so the water fraction falls below 93 percent.
The sodium dissolved in the water is unchanged, so direct ISE stays normal.
But indirect ISE still assumes 93 percent water, so it reports a falsely low sodium. This is pseudohyponatremia, the electrolyte exclusion effect.

In a 2026 study, the sodium bias exceeded analytical limits at a lipemic index of about 300 in spiked samples, and above about 100 in real patients, far below the manufacturer’s stated limit of over 2,000.

scenes.title: Jaffe creatinine and its impostors
scenes.altText: Jaffe card (Pottel 2024; Soleimani 2023; Jiang 2026): creatinine + alkaline picrate → yellow-to-red product read by absorbance. Pseudo-chromogens also react: acetoacetate and other ketone-group substances, pyruvate, proteins, glucose, ascorbic acid → falsely HIGH; fast-reacting α-keto compounds and several cephalosporins (cefoxitin, cephalothin) → falsely HIGH; bilirubin → falsely LOW (negative interference). Enzymatic creatinine: more specific, favoured in ketoacidosis, hyperbilirubinemia and children — but not immune (dopamine, dobutamine, bilirubin, globulin). Back to the hook: Patient 1’s true sodium ≈ 139 (direct ISE); report and flag pseudohyponatremia. Patient 2’s Jaffe creatinine is inflated by acetoacetate — the enzymatic 1.1 is more reliable.

cues.text: The Jaffe method reacts creatinine with alkaline picrate to make a coloured product. But other substances react too.
Acetoacetate and other ketones, pyruvate, glucose and ascorbic acid, plus some cephalosporins, push the result falsely high. Bilirubin pushes it falsely low.
Enzymatic creatinine methods are more specific and are favoured in ketoacidosis, high bilirubin and children, though they have their own interferences, such as dopamine and dobutamine.
Back to patient one: the direct-ISE sodium of 139 is the true value. The indirect result is pseudohyponatremia.
Patient two: acetoacetate inflated the Jaffe creatinine. The enzymatic value of 1.1 is more reliable, so this is not necessarily kidney injury.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Low sodium with TG 2,000 = treat hyponatremia” (✓ indirect ISE pseudohyponatremia — check direct ISE); “Rising Jaffe creatinine in DKA = acute kidney injury” (✓ acetoacetate inflates Jaffe — check enzymatic creatinine); “The manufacturer’s lipemia limit guarantees accuracy” (✓ sodium bias can exceed limits at much lower lipemic indices).

cues.text: Trap one: a low sodium with triglycerides of 2,000 needs hyponatremia treatment. First suspect pseudohyponatremia from indirect ISE, and check a direct ISE sodium.
Trap two: a rising Jaffe creatinine in ketoacidosis means acute kidney injury. Acetoacetate inflates Jaffe creatinine; check an enzymatic method.
Trap three: the manufacturer’s lipemia limit guarantees an accurate sodium. Real-world bias exceeded analytical limits at far lower lipemic indices.

scenes.title: Indirect assumes; Jaffe accepts impostors
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Indirect ISE ASSUMES the water; Jaffe ACCEPTS impostors.” Tokens: Fat/protein ↑ → indirect Na ↓ · Ketones/glucose/cephalosporins → Jaffe ↑ · Bilirubin → Jaffe ↓. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: indirect ISE assumes the water, and Jaffe accepts impostors. Extra fat or protein makes indirect sodium falsely low. Ketones, glucose and some cephalosporins make Jaffe creatinine falsely high, while bilirubin makes it falsely low.
Where it breaks: low protein can push indirect results the other way; compensated Jaffe methods reduce some errors but not all; and enzymatic creatinine has its own interferents.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Indirect ISE dilutes and assumes 93% water → high lipid/protein gives pseudohyponatremia; direct ISE gives the true value”, “Jaffe creatinine: ↑ ketones, glucose, pyruvate, ascorbate, cephalosporins; ↓ bilirubin → use enzymatic creatinine”.

cues.text: Indirect ISE assumes plasma is 93 percent water, so marked lipemia or hyperproteinemia gives pseudohyponatremia that direct ISE avoids, and the Jaffe creatinine reaction is fooled by ketones and bilirubin where enzymatic methods are more specific.

props.label: Indirect ISE: 93% water assumed → lipid/protein ↑ = pseudo-low Na; direct ISE true
Jaffe: ↑ ketones, glucose, cephalosporins · ↓ bilirubin → enzymatic

explanation.what: Plain language: some lab methods make assumptions — indirect sodium assumes plasma is mostly water, and the Jaffe creatinine reaction also reacts with look-alike chemicals — so certain patients get false results that a different method avoids. Scientific terms: ion-selective electrode (direct, indirect), plasma water fraction, electrolyte exclusion effect, pseudohyponatremia, lipemic index, Jaffe reaction (alkaline picrate), pseudo-chromogens, enzymatic creatinine.
explanation.why: Sodium is dissolved only in plasma water. Indirect ISE dilutes the sample and back-calculates assuming ~93% water; when lipid or protein takes up more volume, the assumption over-corrects and sodium reads low. Picrate reacts with ketone-group compounds and other chromogens, raising apparent creatinine; bilirubin interferes negatively.
explanation.measure: Indirect ISE dilutes 1:5–1:46 and assumes ~93% plasma water (Chopra 2026; van Dongen 2026). Lipemia: sodium bias exceeded analytical limits at L-index ~300 (spiked) and > 100 (clinical), below manufacturer claims (> 2,000) (van Dongen 2026). Jaffe pseudo-chromogens: acetoacetate, pyruvate, ketones, proteins, glucose, ascorbic acid (Pottel 2024); cephalosporins and α-keto compounds positive, bilirubin negative (Soleimani 2023; Jiang 2026). Enzymatic favoured in bilirubin, ketoacidosis, children (Pottel 2024).
explanation.differs: Direct ISE (undiluted; true plasma-water activity) vs indirect ISE (diluted; water-fraction assumption). Jaffe (non-specific) vs enzymatic creatinine (more specific; different interferents).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: low sodium with high triglycerides or protein on indirect ISE, DKA with high Jaffe creatinine, bilirubin effect on Jaffe, and the confirmatory method.

right.label: Indirect ISE
points: Falsely low Na in high lipid/protein

mnemonic.text: Indirect ISE ASSUMES the water; Jaffe ACCEPTS impostors.
mnemonic.explanation: Indirect ISE assumes 93% water (pseudohyponatremia when lipid/protein is high); Jaffe reacts with ketones, glucose, cephalosporins (falsely high) and is lowered by bilirubin.
mnemonic.limitation: Low protein can bias indirect ISE the other way; compensated Jaffe methods fix only some errors; enzymatic methods have their own interferents.

analogyLimitations: Beaker drawings of plasma water are schematic.
The patients and values are invented.
“Low protein biases the other way” is stated as a limitation only, not quantified here.
takeaway: Indirect ISE assumes plasma is 93 percent water, so marked lipemia or hyperproteinemia gives pseudohyponatremia that direct ISE avoids, and the Jaffe creatinine reaction is fooled by ketones and bilirubin where enzymatic methods are more specific.

questions.stem: A patient with triglycerides of 3,000 mg/dL has sodium 125 mmol/L on the chemistry analyzer (indirect ISE). What is the best next step?

options.text: Measure sodium by direct ISE (e.g., blood-gas analyzer)
options.rationale: Correct. Direct ISE measures undiluted sample and is not affected by the reduced plasma water fraction.
Incorrect. Severe lipemia causes pseudohyponatremia on indirect ISE.

options.text: Repeat on the same indirect ISE analyzer
options.rationale: Incorrect. The bias is systematic and will recur.

options.text: Dilute the sample further and rerun
options.rationale: Incorrect. Indirect ISE already dilutes; the error comes from the water-fraction assumption.

questions.stem: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a Jaffe creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL that falls to 1.0 mg/dL by an enzymatic method. What explains the difference?

options.text: Acetoacetate reacting with alkaline picrate (positive interference)
options.rationale: Correct. Ketone-group compounds are Jaffe pseudo-chromogens.

options.text: Acute kidney injury that resolved between tests
options.rationale: Incorrect. The difference is between methods on the same patient, pointing to analytical interference.

options.text: Dopamine interference in the Jaffe assay
options.rationale: Incorrect. Dopamine is listed as an interferent of enzymatic, not Jaffe, methods.

questions.stem: Which substance causes NEGATIVE interference in the Jaffe creatinine method?

options.rationale: Correct. Bilirubin and its breakdown products lower Jaffe creatinine.
Incorrect. Glucose is a slow-reacting positive interferent.
Incorrect. Cephalosporins such as cefoxitin raise Jaffe creatinine.

Enzymatic creatinine more specific; own interferents; favoured settings.

accuracyFlags.issue: Manufacturer lipemia limits for sodium may be far higher than the indices at which clinically relevant bias occurs (van Dongen 2026, single-centre, one analyzer). Laboratories should verify their own limits.
